options.why: Reads the base correctly as a pentagon but calls the solid a pyramid, ignoring the two matching bases and the absence of an apex.
Counts all $7$ faces of the solid ($5$ side faces plus $2$ bases) and uses that total as the number of sides on the base.
Uses the total of $7$ faces as the base name and also picks the pyramid family because the side faces look slanted.

questions.solution_text: The matching bases are pentagons, so it is a pentagonal prism.

options.why: Uses prism even though the solid has one base and an apex.
Names the triangular side faces instead of the base.
Uses a broad base description and the wrong family.

questions.solution_text: The solid has a square base and an apex, so it is a square pyramid.

questions.question_text:
A prism has two matching hexagonal ends.
What is its name?

options.why: Keeps the base name but ignores that there are two matching bases.
Names the joining side faces instead of the bases.
Uses informal wording and changes the solid family.

questions.solution_text: A prism is named after its base, which is a hexagon.

questions.question_text:
A pyramid has $8$ triangular side faces.
What is its name?

options.why: Matches the $8$ side faces to an octagonal base correctly but chooses the prism family even though the faces are triangles meeting at an apex.
Subtracts one from the side-face count, computing $8 - 1 = 7$, as if one face were the base.
Subtracts one from the side-face count, $8 - 1 = 7$, and also names the prism family instead of the pyramid family.

questions.solution_text: Eight triangular side faces meet the eight sides of an octagonal base.

questions.question_text:
A prism has $12$ vertices.
What is its name?

options.why: Halves the vertex count correctly to get $12 \div 2 = 6$ base vertices but then names the pyramid family instead of the prism family.
Uses the total vertex count of $12$ as the number of sides on one base, forgetting the vertices are shared between two bases.
Uses all $12$ vertices as the base's sides and also names the pyramid family instead of the prism family.

questions.solution_text: The two bases share the $12$ vertices equally, so each is a hexagon.

questions.question_text: Which name can also describe a cube?

options.why: A cube has no apex and has two matching square bases.
A cube has square, not triangular, bases.
Uses a pyramid name for a solid with no apex.

questions.solution_text: A cube has two identical parallel square bases, so it is a square prism.
